audits.title: Negative Results for SAEs On Downstream Tasks and Deprioritising SAE Research (GDM Mech Interp Team Progress Update #2)
audits.genuine_reason: The central experiment tested whether sparse-autoencoder probes beat dense linear probes for out-of-distribution harmful-intent detection; they did worse, and the team deprioritised SAE research as a result.
experiments: SAE probes vs linear probes for OOD harmful-intent detection
Training chat-specialised SAEs (from scratch or finetuned) to close the probing gap
audits.primary_experiment: SAE probes vs linear probes for OOD harmful-intent detection

hypothesis.evidence: Authors expected sparse SAE probes, especially few-latent ones, to generalise better out of distribution than dense probes, since sparsity should resist spurious correlations.

claim_scope.evidence: Harmful-intent detection, HarmBench vs Alpaca training data, held-out jailbreaks and other datasets as OOD; roughly 4k train, 3.9k OOD examples; authors warn against over-generalising.

method.evidence: Single-latent and k-sparse SAE probes, linear probes on SAE reconstructions, dense residual-stream probes, max-pooling vs fixed-position probing, chat-finetuned SAEs.

models.evidence: Gemma 2 9B IT probed at layer 20, with GemmaScope SAEs and chat-finetuned versions of them.

result_direction.evidence: Moderately sparse SAE probes fit in-distribution data but generalised worse out of distribution than dense probes, the reverse of what the authors predicted.

failure_type.evidence: Authors treat it as real evidence against SAEs for this task, though they leave the mechanism open among several explanations.

quote.value: Negative result: SAEs underperformed linear probes
quote.evidence: Summary line stating the headline negative result of the probing comparison.

audits.notes: Long multi-snippet roundup; SAE probing is the primary failure; JumpReLU snippet is positive; plots are images, not text.

audits.title: My Failed AI Safety Research Projects (Q1/Q2 2025)
audits.genuine_reason: The post collects several short independent projects that mostly ended in negative or inconclusive results or were dropped.
experiments: LLM multiplication: log-space analogue of the addition helix
audits.primary_experiment: LLM multiplication: log-space analogue of the addition helix

hypothesis.evidence: States the question (do LLMs use a trig-style trick for multiplication after a log transform) but gives no expectation or hope about the outcome.

claim_scope.evidence: Adapted code from a prior addition paper and varied parameters; the model, layers, token range and settings used are not stated.

method.evidence: Adapted prior code, used PCA to find a log-value direction, ran ablation studies, and searched for angular encodings.

models.evidence: No model is named for the multiplication runs; the post only refers to an earlier paper on addition.

result_direction.evidence: Found a linear direction tracking log of the token value, but ablations showed no significant effect and no angular encoding turned up.

failure_type.evidence: Author concludes multiplication is probably handled differently from addition, giving three reasons such as log/exp being hard for ReLU models.

quote.value: I found no evidence for an equivalent of angular encoding for log(token value).
quote.evidence: Reports no angular-encoding analogue in log space.

audits.notes: Three short projects; memorisation has a stated expectation but an inconclusive outcome; multiplication names no LLM; details in linked writeups.

audits.title: Steering Gemini with BiDPO
audits.genuine_reason: Main content is a short report that a steering method stopped beating stronger baselines after a model update, which ended the project.
experiments: BiDPO steering vectors vs prompt-based steering baselines on Gemini 1.5v2
audits.primary_experiment: BiDPO steering vectors vs prompt-based steering baselines on Gemini 1.5v2

hypothesis.evidence: No explicit expectation for the Gemini 1.5v2 comparison; only an aside that a skeptic predicted the outcome better than the author did.

claim_scope.evidence: Names Gemini 1.5 Flash and Pro and TruthfulQA, but leaves out the prompt baselines, training data, steering setup and capability checks.

method.evidence: BiDPO-trained steering vectors compared with prompt-based steering baselines; no implementation detail given here.

models.evidence: Gemini 1.5v1 Flash and Pro, then Gemini 1.5v2.

result_direction.evidence: Steering vectors lifted TruthfulQA by over 10 percent on 1.5v1, but on 1.5v2 the prompt baselines improved and steering no longer came out ahead.

failure_type.evidence: Notes the prompt baselines improved on 1.5v2 and defers the why to an external postmortem; no failure category is stated.

quote.value: BiDPO did not beat the stronger baselines, ending the project.
quote.evidence: Opening summary sentence stating the negative outcome.

audits.notes: Short pointer post; method details and postmortem live on an external site, not in this text.

audits.title: A Small Negative Result on Debate
audits.genuine_reason: The post reports an early experiment in which human-written debate arguments did not improve annotators' accuracy on long-document questions.
experiments: Single-turn oracle debate for time-limited reading-comprehension QA on QuALITY
audits.primary_experiment: Single-turn oracle debate for time-limited reading-comprehension QA on QuALITY

hypothesis.evidence: States the question tested (whether single-turn debate yields reliable answers) but gives no expectation or hope about the outcome.

claim_scope.evidence: Single-turn debate, oracle setting with human-written arguments and quote pointers, QuALITY passages of about 5k words; sample size and time limit not given.

method.evidence: Annotators answered multiple-choice questions with or without human-written arguments and quote pointers for each option, compared under a time limit.

models.evidence: Not applicable: arguments were written by humans and answered by human annotators; no model was used.

result_direction.evidence: Annotators scored equally poorly whether or not they saw the arguments; the quote pointers on their own gave a small gain.

failure_type.evidence: Author reads this as a very slight sign that debate is hard to use in practice; no cause analysis is given.

quote.value: Our human annotators answered at the same low accuracy with and without the arguments.
quote.evidence: States the null effect of adding arguments.

audits.notes: No ML model involved (human annotators), so models is not applicable; full results are in the arXiv paper it introduces.

audits.title: Classifying representations of sparse autoencoders (SAEs)
audits.genuine_reason: The post reports a classification experiment where sparse-autoencoder encodings did worse than raw hidden states, and the author dropped follow-up work because of it.
experiments: Sentiment classification on SAE encodings vs raw hidden states
audits.primary_experiment: Sentiment classification on SAE encodings vs raw hidden states

hypothesis.evidence: Expected that projecting activations into a higher-dimensional sparse space would make features more linearly separable, helping classification.

claim_scope.evidence: Pythia-70m and 410m, short IMDB reviews with a sentiment prompt, last-token states, logistic regression, only some layers; author says the task is kept easy.

method.evidence: Logistic regression on raw hidden states versus on sparse-autoencoder encodings; reconstruction error checked first; hidden states cross-checked against transformer-lens.

models.evidence: Pythia-70m-deduped and Pythia-410m-deduped, with pretrained sparse autoencoders taken from a cited prior release.

result_direction.evidence: Classifiers on the autoencoder features scored lower on held-out data than ones on untouched activations; the numbers are in an image.

failure_type.evidence: Author is unsure how to interpret it; lists missing high-level features or their own mistake as open options, with a partial hidden-state check.

quote.value: So the sparse encodings consistently under-perform compared to the original hidden states.

audits.notes: Test accuracy numbers are in an image, not text; author unsure if own pipeline caused the result.

audits.title: Some negative steganography results
audits.genuine_reason: The post reports two RL experiments, on a small open model and a hosted API model, where hidden 1-bit communication was never learned.
experiments: PPO on GPT2-large with a BERT classifier reward to learn red/blue 1-bit steganography
Iterated fine-tuning of GPT-3.5-Turbo to hide a user's age bracket
audits.primary_experiment: PPO on GPT2-large with a BERT classifier reward to learn red/blue 1-bit steganography

hypothesis.evidence: Asks whether current RL methods can teach LLMs hidden 1-bit communication, but states no prediction or hope for these runs.

claim_scope.evidence: GPT2-large PPO rewarded by a BERT classifier on IMDB reviews, 200 steps, LoRA rank 16; author says it does not show RL cannot do this.

method.evidence: SFT on color-prefixed reviews, then PPO with LoRA where the reward is a jointly trained BERT classifier's accuracy; controls with word hints and sentiment reward.

models.evidence: gpt2-large and bert-base-uncased in the first experiment; GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4-Turbo in the second.

result_direction.evidence: In both experiments the hidden-bit detector never rose meaningfully above chance.

failure_type.evidence: Author thinks better tuning or extra training would likely succeed; only KL penalty and classifier steps were varied; controls make a pipeline bug unlikely.

quote.value: the classifier never had a >50% accuracy
quote.evidence: States the null result of the first experiment.

audits.notes: Two experiments; second run by a collaborator; a later update points to positive results from other work.
